title: In essentials, unity
hookLine: an old motto: in essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity

cards: In essentials, unity. In non-essentials, liberty. In all things, charity.
Three short lines, sometimes lettered on a church wall or printed in a bulletin. People like to hang the motto on well-known names; who first wrote it is less certain than the motto itself.

What's clear is who it was written for: Christians who disagreed, sometimes bitterly, and still had to share a city, a table, a faith. After a block of honest disagreements, it's a good place to stand.

teach.b: The idea is older than the motto. Paul faced it in his letter to Rome. Some believers ate meat; others ate only herbs.

Some kept certain days as holy; others treated every day alike. They were starting to look down on each other. Paul's answer opens like this: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations."
Welcome each other, and don't turn the welcome into a debate. And then: "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind." Food and days, for Paul, were not things to split over.
Who decides what counts as essential? Churches don't share one list. Some point to the creeds.
Some to the plain teaching of scripture about Christ. Catholics and Orthodox to the teaching the church has received and handed on. Even the list of essentials is something Christians disagree about.
Which is why the last line carries so much weight.

teach.h: HAVE NOT CHARITY, I AM NOTHING.
teach.b: In Paul's chapter on love, charity is the King James word for love, and the chapter is blunt: "though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing." All faith.
Even right faith, on every essential. Without love, nothing.

teach.h: KEEP THE UNITY OF THE SPIRIT.
teach.b: So the letter to the Ephesians asks for effort: "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." Unity there isn't a feeling that happens on its own. It's something kept, on purpose.

how: Christians from different churches can be found working and praying together on what they hold in common, such as the creeds, the Lord's Prayer and service to neighbors, while keeping their own teaching on matters where they differ.

o: agreement on every detail of church life
unity on what matters most in the faith
the basic supplies a church keeps on hand

games.q: the motto and the text — tap the pairs.

s: in Romans 14, Paul's example is about food and holy days
some ate meat, some only herbs; some kept certain days. not things to split over, he says.
charity in the King James means giving money
it's the word for love: "and have not charity, I am nothing."
churches share one agreed list of essentials
some point to the creeds, some to scripture's plain teaching, some to the church's received teaching. even the list needs charity.

games.q: you're in Rome in Paul's day. one friend eats only herbs; another eats meat; they've started to look down on each other. what does Paul tell them?
o: the meat-eater is right; the other should change.
receive one another, and don't turn it into a debate.
stop eating together until it's settled.
games.why: "him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations." each is to be "fully persuaded in his own mind."

practice: Choose one real disagreement, with a relative, a friend, a church, a stranger online, and ask: is this essential, or not?

Whatever you decide, find one good thing the other person is trying to protect, and hold it a while without giving up your own view. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just wish them well.

wordCard.voice: In essentials. The first line of an old motto: unity on what matters most, liberty on the rest, and charity, which is love, over everything.

orig.note: Greek: love; the word the King James renders charity in 1 Corinthians 13.

carryVoice: Your line: in all things, charity. The motto's last line, and its heaviest. Go gently.
